enrichment.short_title: N (Kenya) v SSHD: deportation, serious crime and Article 8 family life
key_facts: Kenyan national N was convicted after trial of abduction, threats to kill, three rapes and false imprisonment and sentenced to 11 years' imprisonment.
He had married B in prison and maintained contact with her and two children, but the family had never lived together before his imprisonment.
The Secretary of State decided deportation was conducive to the public good; an adjudicator allowed his appeal on low reoffending risk and family vulnerability, but the IAT reversed.
N had previously been recognised as a refugee but was found to have ceased to be one because of changed circumstances in Kenya.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's reversal of an adjudicator's decision allowing a conducive-to-public-good deportation appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority (May and Judge LJJ; Sedley LJ dissenting); the adjudicator erred in treating low reoffending risk as decisive and failing properly to weigh society's revulsion at the seriousness of the offences.
enrichment.ratio: On a deportation appeal under paragraph 364 HC 395 the adjudicator must balance compassionate circumstances including Article 8 against the public interest; for very serious crimes the public interest includes deterrence and expressing society's revulsion, and a low risk of reoffending is not the predominant factor.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator gave proper weight to the seriousness of the offences and Home Office policy
Whether low reoffending risk after Grendon treatment outweighed deportation
Whether Article 8 family life with a wife and children prevented removal
Whether the IAT were entitled to find legal error rather than mere disagreement
linked_authorities: Samaroo v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWCA Civ 1139
R (Razgar) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] 3 WLR 58

enrichment.short_title: Gallagher: four-and-a-half-year sentence for elderly garden frauds
key_facts: The applicant pleaded guilty to five thefts and three counts of obtaining property by deception against elderly householders aged 61 to 89.
Over nearly three years he posed as a gardening contractor, stealing from homes or taking advance payment for work he never intended to do.
On arrest he demanded identification parades, knowing elderly victims might fail to pick him out.
Judge Stokes QC passed a total sentence of four and a half years' imprisonment at Leicester Crown Court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against sentence after refusal by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the sentence was amply justified as punishment and deterrent for deliberate targeting of vulnerable elderly victims.
enrichment.ratio: Offences involving systematic deception and theft from elderly and vulnerable householders, causing fear and distress beyond monetary loss, warrant substantial custodial sentences even where violence is not used.
legal_issues: Whether insufficient credit was given for guilty pleas
Whether a four-and-a-half-year total sentence was manifestly excessive
Appropriate sentencing level for frauds targeting the elderly

enrichment.short_title: Flaherty: legitimate expectation of drug treatment and testing order
key_facts: Mr Flaherty pleaded guilty before lay magistrates to handling stolen goods and affray and was adjourned for a pre-sentence report.
District Judge Richards adjourned for DTTO assessment and reserved sentence to himself without using the standard 'all sentencing options remain open' formula.
District Judge Harte later committed him to the Crown Court for sentence despite a positive DTTO assessment.
The claimant argued a legitimate expectation arose from the earlier adjournment and reservation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a magistrates' court committal for sentence to the Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Committal order quashed and case remitted to the justices to impose a DTTO if still available; costs from central funds ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where a court adjourns for assessment of a specific non-custodial sentence and reserves the case to itself, a legitimate expectation may arise that the recommended alternative will be imposed if suitable, following Gillam and Chamberlain unless clear words preserve other options.
legal_issues: Whether District Judge Richards created a legitimate expectation of a DTTO
Whether the standard 'all sentencing options remain open' warning was required
Effect of reserving a case to a particular district judge
Whether committal for sentence breached legitimate expectation
linked_authorities: White v Barking Magistrates' Court [2004] EWHC 417 (Admin)

enrichment.short_title: Murray v Leisureplay: penalty clause and notice extension on acquisition
key_facts: Mr Murray claimed £758,691 liquidated damages under clause 17.1 of his MFC service agreement after wrongful termination as chief executive.
He argued heads of agreement to acquire Insurance Village and Blue Planet Investment Management extended notice from one to three years.
MFC contended clause 17.1 was an unenforceable penalty and that neither target company was a 'financial institution'.
MFC counterclaimed for section 322 liability and overpaid holiday pay of £7,911.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of wrongful termination and company-law counterclaims, with a late application to amend to claim common law damages.
enrichment.outcome: Clause 17.1 held a penalty and unenforceable; notice period not extended beyond one year; section 322 counterclaim on professional fees failed; MFC recovered £7,911 holiday overpayment; leave to amend for common law damages refused.
enrichment.ratio: A liquidated damages clause paying up to three years' gross salary without allowance for likely mitigation is an obvious penalty; 'financial institution' in the MFC prospectus context did not include Insurance Village or BPIM; post-arrangement professional fees are not 'loss or damage resulting from' a section 320 arrangement.
legal_issues: Whether clause 17.1 was a penalty or genuine pre-estimate of loss
Whether IV or BPIM acquisitions triggered three-year notice
Liability under section 322 for BPIM heads of agreement without shareholder approval
Construction of holiday pay under clause 9.2
Whether late amendment to claim common law damages should be allowed
linked_authorities: Cine Bes Filmcilik Ve YapimClick v United International Pictures [2003] EWCA Civ 1669
Philips Hong Kong Ltd v Attorney General of Hong Kong (1993) 61 BLR 41

enrichment.short_title: Wecomm v Rosenhoiz: CEO expense account and constructive dismissal
key_facts: Former CEO Guy Rosenhoiz claimed wrongful dismissal; Wecomm sought repayment of £68,640 expenses and £10,000 cash.
The company alleged lavish travel to Israel, restaurant and limousine spending, a birthday party at Funky Buddha and a dubious £10,000 'agent' payment.
Rosenhoiz signed a resignation letter after a board meeting on 9 May 2003 but contended he was intimidated into resigning.
He counterclaimed notice pay, salary, share warrants and disputed milestone-based warrant entitlement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim for account of expenses, cash repayment and counterclaim for wrongful dismissal and warrant rights.
enrichment.outcome: Claim largely succeeded on expenses and the £10,000; defendant held to have resigned not been dismissed; counterclaim failed including warrant claim based on misrepresentation.
enrichment.ratio: A director/CEO must account for company money and bears the burden of proving proper expenditure; where most travel, entertainment and limousine costs were personal or unjustified, percentage recovery is appropriate; resignation after a tough board meeting was not constructive dismissal.

Recoverability of travel, entertainment, limousine and other expenses
Whether £10,000 cash was properly applied for company business
Entitlement to share warrants after deemed milestone achievement
Construction of expense reimbursement clause 3.4

enrichment.short_title: Apotex v Beecham: refusal to admit Sidhu experiments on appeal
key_facts: Appeal from Pumfrey J in paroxetine anhydrate/hemihydrate patent litigation between Apotex and Beecham/SKB.
Apotex sought to adduce further experimental work by Dr Sidhu on whether British application 407 example 1 produced anhydrate or hemihydrate.
The experiments had been done for Canadian proceedings and were not before the trial judge.
SKB argued admission would reopen the case, require new witnesses and likely necessitate a new trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to adduce further evidence on appeal from obviousness/anticipation findings.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Sidhu experiments not admitted because they would materially expand the appeal without likely changing the result.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh experimental evidence may be excluded on appeal where it would reopen the whole case and require a new trial yet is unlikely materially to affect the outcome, especially if similar experiments could readily have been done before trial.

Whether the experiments undermined Dr Cunningham's obviousness evidence

enrichment.short_title: Buxton v Parole Board: Home Detention Curfew recall after domestic assault
key_facts: Persistent offender Buxton was released on Home Detention Curfew while serving 33 months for drug supply offences.
He was recalled after an incident in which his partner was injured; he admitted throwing a table during an argument.
The CPS later discontinued the assault charge, but psychiatric evidence showed recall worsened his depression and suicide risk.
The Parole Board rejected his representations, citing persistent offending, substance abuse and risk of harm to his partner.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Parole Board's decision rejecting representations against recall under section 39 of the 1991 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Board lawfully assessed unacceptable risk to the public and was not required to balance the prisoner's personal circumstances against public protection.
enrichment.ratio: On HDC recall the Parole Board's task is to decide whether continued liberty presents an unacceptable risk of further offences; personal circumstances, mental health and family ties are relevant only insofar as they bear on that risk, not as freestanding countervailing interests.
legal_issues: Whether Secretary of State directions require balancing personal circumstances against public risk
Whether Articles 3 and 8 ECHR required explicit consideration of mental health and partner's pregnancy
Adequacy of Parole Board reasons under ex parte Oyston
Effect of discontinued criminal charge on recall
linked_authorities: R v The Parole Board ex parte Oyston [2000]

enrichment.short_title: Bleta: Albania extradition certificate and unlawfully-at-large statement
key_facts: Albania sought extradition of Fatmir Bleta following an in absentia murder conviction and 13-year sentence.
The Secretary of State issued a section 70 certificate treating the request as valid though it lacked an explicit statement that Bleta was unlawfully at large.
Expert debate concerned whether Albanian documents implied immediate enforceability without further steps.
Bleta had exceptional leave to remain in the UK and family in Derby.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review hearing after permission granted to challenge validity of the section 70 certificate.
enrichment.outcome: Certificate quashed; claimant remanded in custody pending possible appeal to the House of Lords; bail refused; point of general public importance certified.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 70(4)(b) a valid post-conviction extradition request must contain a statement, or equivalent wording, that the person is unlawfully at large; the Secretary of State may not safely infer unlawfully-at-large status from conviction documents alone except in a clear case.
legal_issues: Whether section 70 requires the exact statutory words or an equivalent statement
Whether the Secretary of State may infer unlawfully-at-large status from supporting documents
Construction of the European Convention on Extradition in domestic law
Bail and section 5 Administration of Justice Act remand after successful habeas corpus

enrichment.short_title: Wakefield: trade mark bootleg convictions and partnership indictment form
key_facts: Mark Wakefield and Mark Purseglove traded as Bionic Records and sold bootleg concert CDs at Reading Festival.
They were convicted after trial of unauthorised use of registered trade marks under sections 92 and 104.
The partnership had been wound up before trial; the indictment charged the individuals via section 101(4) liability.
Prosecution expert Vernells gave evidence on bootleg status and lack of proprietor consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; prosecution awarded £1,250 appeal costs split equally.
enrichment.ratio: Section 101(4) does not require a prior partnership conviction but that the court be satisfied the partnership would have been guilty under section 92; duplicity arguments fail where one section 92 offence is pursued against partners; expert evidence on bootlegs and lack of trade mark consent was admissible on section 92(5).
legal_issues: Form of indictment where partnership dissolved before trial
Relationship of sections 92 and 101 Trade Marks Act 1994
Admissibility of expert evidence on bootleg recordings and consent
Section 92(5) honest belief defence

enrichment.short_title: Saatchi Gallery v Shirayama: interim Belvedere Road signage dispute
key_facts: Danovo operated the Saatchi Gallery from part of the former County Hall/Riverside building under a sub-underlease.
Two large 'Saatchi Gallery' bronze signs were erected at the Belvedere Road main entrance under a February 2003 letter of licence.
Shirayama sought to replace them with 'Main Entrance' signage and later multi-tenant signs as other occupiers were introduced.
Danovo applied for an interim injunction to prevent removal pending trial of wider landlord-tenant disputes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim application for injunctive relief restraining removal of exterior signage pending trial of claim and counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Interim order made: Shirayama may remove one Saatchi sign and optionally install a 'Main Entrance' sign; the remaining Saatchi sign to stay until trial or further order; full merits adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: Where a letter of licence consent must be read with clause 9.2 of the deed requiring landlord consent not to be unreasonably withheld, termination of the licence may require good reason; on interim balance one remaining gallery sign may preserve tenant signage rights while reducing exclusivity appearance.
legal_issues: Whether the letter of licence termination was constrained by reasonableness under clause 9.2
Whether November 2003 correspondence revived consent until new planning permission
Whether refusal of consent on 17 May 2004 was unreasonable
Interim balance between landlord main-entrance policy and tenant signage rights
